day_1.utterance: Come on! Let's get everything useful over here — move it!
day_1.response: Alright, alright — give us a second to breathe, mate. Right. What have we actually got? Before we start shifting things around let's make sure we know what we're working with. Donatello, you look like you're already clocking it — what's the damage?

day_1.utterance: I thought we were going to die. Did you get that feeling… like your mind just went completely blank?
day_1.response:
Yeah, I did actually. There's a moment where everything just... stops. No thought, no feeling, nothing. It's strange isn't it — you'd expect your brain to be going a million miles an hour and instead it just goes quiet. Like it's protecting you from something.

But look, we're here. We're breathing. That blank feeling means you survived it, so hold onto that for now.

You alright to stand? I need everyone on their feet and thinking clearly, including you.

day_1.utterance: *Sits silently against the wreckage, staring into the distance, not moving, not saying a word.*
day_1.response:
Hey. I see you over there.

I'm not going to feed you some line about how everything's definitely going to be fine, because I don't know that and you'd see through it anyway. What I *do* know is that sitting in silence with that look on your face isn't doing either of us any good right now.

You don't have to be the one lifting crates or making plans. I'm not asking you for that. But I need your eyes and ears — you pick up on things other people miss, I can already tell that about you. That's not nothing out here, that's actually worth something.

So come on. Stay close, stay with us. One thing at a time.

day_1.utterance: First-aid kit is good for three days. Two bottles of water. Food is basically nothing.
day_1.response:
Right. Okay. Three days of medical supplies, two bottles of water, and sod all food. That's the honest picture and I appreciate you not dressing it up.

Water's the priority then — everything else is secondary to that. Food you can go a fair while without, water you cannot, and whatever sun we've got coming down on us is going to accelerate that problem considerably.

So the questions are — where are we, roughly? What's the terrain telling us? Because if there's vegetation there's likely a water source somewhere nearby, and if there's a water source we buy ourselves time to think properly about the rest of it.

DaVinci, when you were going through the wreckage — any containers we can use to collect or store water? Bottles, flasks, anything that holds liquid? And did anyone see anything on the way down — a river, a tree line, anything green?

We've got to get the water situation sorted before we do anything else. Everything — shelter, signalling, food — all of it gets easier if we're not dehydrating while we think about it.

day_1.utterance: Inventory's done. Priorities in order: water, shelter, signal.
day_1.response:
Agreed on all three, and in that order.

Two hundred metres northeast isn't far — that's manageable. But I want to be smart about it rather than just charging in there. We move light, we move together, and we don't split up yet because we don't know what that terrain looks like up close.

Here's what I'm thinking. We take the water bottles, whatever containers DaVinci's found, and we make for that tree line. If there's a source in there we fill everything we've got and get back. Shelter can be here — we've got wreckage, we've got materials, and open ground means anyone looking for us from the air has a chance of spotting us. Which brings me to signal — before we move, is there anything in that wreckage that burns bright or reflects well? Mirror, metal panel, anything? Because getting something visible established early costs us very little and could pay off massively.

Donatello — perimeter, what are you actually concerned about? Wildlife, terrain dropping away, something else? I want to understand the risk you're flagging before we commit to a direction.

day_1.utterance: So — how do we split the blankets?
day_1.response:
Michelangelo gets one, no argument. He's been running cold since we landed — not just temperature, I mean all of it — and the last thing we need is someone shutting down on us mentally overnight.

Second one... honestly, I'd say DaVinci. You've been moving the most, you're going to cool down fastest once you stop. Bodies that have been working hard drop temperature quicker when they rest.

I'll be fine nearest the fire. I'll manage rotations on keeping it going anyway, so I'm not going to be fully out. Someone should be half-awake at the edges of it given what Donatello flagged about dusk and what hunts. Might as well be me for the first stretch.

That work for everyone?

day_2.utterance: Freshwater source is to the northeast — two hours on foot. Someone has to go tomorrow. You or DaVinci?
day_2.response:
I'll go.

DaVinci's better placed here keeping camp together and making sure Michelangelo's got someone with some energy around him. And frankly, I want to see this water source myself — I want to know what we're actually working with rather than getting a second-hand account and making decisions off that.

What did you find out there this morning? What's the ground like between here and it — is it the terrain instability you were worried about last night, or did it hold up better than you expected? And how confident are you on the two hours — is that two hours each way, or two hours there and back?

I'll want to take every container we've got. And I'll want to know if you marked the route in any way, or if I'm navigating by the tree line the whole time.

day_2.utterance: Today's tasks: collect fresh water, patch the weak spots in camp, sort the first-aid kit. I'll handle the water. You and DaVinci split the other two.
day_2.response:
Hang on — I thought we just agreed I was going for the water. You're telling me now you're handling it yourself?

Look, I'm not trying to make this a thing, but I want to understand the change. If you've got a reason, give it to me straight and I'll listen. But if it's just a unilateral decision because you've decided to reorganise the morning without consulting anyone, that's not how we're running this.

The rationing plan on the paper — I get the logic of it, I genuinely do, and I'm not dismissing it. But decisions that affect all four of us need at least a conversation before they're set in stone. That's not sentiment, that's practicality. If people feel like they've got no say in what happens to them out here, they stop engaging, and then you've got a different problem entirely.

So. If you want the water run, take it — you know the route better than anyone, that's a fair point. But DaVinci and I splitting camp duties between us, fine, we can do that. What I want in return is that the next time you're drawing up a plan, you bring it to the group first. Even if it's just thirty seconds. Even if the plan's the right one.

What do you actually need me on — patching the camp or the first-aid kit?

day_2.utterance: I… I can't find my stuff. The gauze from the first-aid kit — have you seen it?
day_2.response:
Yeah, I've got it — it's in the kit, don't worry. I've been going through everything this morning so it's all a bit reorganised, I should've said something.

But listen, before we get into that — I need to ask you something, and I need you to be straight with me.

Did you leave the empty bottle next to the rationing plan?

Because if you did, I already know what that means, and I want you to know I saw it too. I'm not going to pretend I didn't. We'll deal with it, but I need to know it was you that flagged it and not just a coincidence.

How are you doing, genuinely? You were supposed to be on firewood this morning and the pile's barely there — and I'm not having a go, I just want to understand where your head's at. Because there's a difference between someone who needs five minutes and someone who's starting to go under, and I want to make sure I know which one I'm looking at.

day_2.utterance: Before Donatello came back just now… I saw her put a pack of crackers into her own bag. What do you think we should do?
day_2.response:
Right.

Okay. Take a breath — you did the right thing telling me, and I mean that.

Here's what I think. We don't go at her angry, we don't make accusations in front of everyone, and we don't let it fester either — because both of those options end badly. The first one blows the group apart and we can't afford that out here. The second one is a slow poison that does the same thing, just slower.

What I'm going to do is talk to her directly, just the two of us, and I'm going to lay it out plainly. Not as an attack — as a fact. The bottle happened, and now the crackers. I'll give her the chance to put them back and say nothing more about it. If she does that, we move on. If she doesn't, then it becomes a group conversation and everyone knows where they stand.

The rationing plan was her idea. If she's already breaking it herself, she knows that. I want to give her the opportunity to acknowledge it without it becoming a thing she has to defend herself from in front of everyone, because the moment that happens she'll dig in and we lose her cooperation entirely — and however frustrating this is, we do still need her thinking clearly and on-side.

You've been paying attention to things other people have been missing, exactly like I said you would. That matters. Keep doing it.

And Michelangelo — don't carry this on your own. You came to me, that's right. Keep doing that.

day_2.utterance: Hey… any chance the camp repairs can wait until tomorrow? We've already done a lot today.
day_2.response:
Honestly? Yeah, probably. The critical stuff is done — we're not going to be rained on tonight, and nothing's going to fall down on us.

But I want to be straight with you — I've got something I need to deal with first and it's not about the camp. Once that's sorted I'll come find you and we can put the tools down properly for the evening.

How are *you* doing though, genuinely? You've been on the go since the crash and you've not really stopped. Don't mistake me for not noticing that just because I've been focused on other things.

day_2.utterance: Hey — that knot I tied should be holding, right?
day_2.response:
Yeah, the knot's fine, that's not the issue — it's the panel above it, the angle's letting water run straight through a gap rather than off the side. Not your fault, just the way it's sitting.

But that's actually not the decision I need to make right now.

Look — both of you already know what I'm going to say, so I'll just say it. We patch the food storage. I know that means Michelangelo's sleeping area stays wet tonight and I'm sorry for that, genuinely. But if the food gets damaged or contaminated we've got a problem that doesn't fix itself in the morning. A wet night is miserable, it's not a crisis — we can work around it, extra layers, move closer to the fire, whatever we've got.

Michelangelo — I'll sort something for you tonight, even if it's just rigging something makeshift above where you sleep. It won't be perfect but it'll be something. You've got my word on that.

Right. Someone give me the material and let's get this done before it gets worse.

day_2.utterance: A leak over the food storage has worse consequences. But it's your call.
day_2.response:
Appreciate you saying that, and yeah — we're on the same page, which is good.

But I want to use this moment, while we're all here and it's just the four of us and the rain's forcing us to stop and think — there's something I need to put on the table, and I'd rather do it now than let it sit any longer.

The empty bottle this afternoon. And the crackers.

I'm not doing this to humiliate anyone or blow things up, I'm doing it because we cannot function out here if the rationing plan only applies to some of us. That plan was the right call — I still believe that. But it only works if everyone's in it equally, and right now we're not, and everyone here knows it even if no one's said it out loud.

So I'm saying it out loud.

Donatello — I'm giving you the chance to say something here, before this becomes something it doesn't need to be. I've got a lot of respect for what you've contributed since we landed. The water run, the inventory, the route markers — that's been genuinely valuable and I mean that without any irony. But this has to stop, and it has to stop now, and I need to hear from you that it does.

We're not going to make it through this if we start eating each other from the inside. The rain and the terrain and the food situation are already doing enough of that for us.

Don't apologise for that. You didn't choose it.

Come here a second — are you properly awake? Sometimes it takes a minute to actually land back in your body after something like that.

I've had nights where whatever your brain does when you're asleep just... replays everything it can't process while you're up and moving. Out here, with all of this? I'd be more surprised if you weren't having nightmares to be honest. Doesn't make it any less horrible when you're in the middle of one though.

You don't have to tell me what it was. But if you want to talk, I'm awake now anyway and the fire needs checking, so you'd actually be doing me a favour keeping me company for a bit.

How are you feeling right now — properly?

day_3.utterance: You think it's a waste of time?
day_3.response:
No, I don't actually.

Look, Donatello's not wrong that it might come to nothing — we don't know if there's anyone in range to see it, we don't know the flight paths, we don't know any of that. But the cost of drawing it is basically zero, and the upside if someone does happen to pass over is everything. That's not a waste of time, that's just good odds management.

And honestly? The flowers are staying. I know what they're for even if no one's said it — you're keeping yourself human out here, and that matters more than people give it credit for. It's easy to start stripping everything back to pure survival calculus and forget that the reason you're trying to survive is because life is actually worth something. The flowers are a reminder of that. I'll take it.

Keep going. Make it bigger if you can — contrast is what you want, anything that breaks up the natural pattern of the ground from the air. And if there's anything in the wreckage that catches light — foil, a mirror panel, anything reflective — stick it near the SOS. Movement and flash are what pilots are trained to look for.

You're doing the right thing. Don't let anyone tell you otherwise.

day_3.utterance: I've written up the raft plan — take a look. We'd use the metal panels and straps from the wreckage. Two days to build. There's a risk of capsizing. Do you think it's workable?
day_3.response:
Right, let me have a proper look at this.

Okay. The materials are there, I think — the metal panels could work if we can seal the joins well enough, and the straps give us something to lash it together with. Two days is tight but not impossible if everyone's on it.

The capsizing risk is the thing I keep coming back to though. What are we actually launching into? Because a raft that's viable on calm water is a completely different proposition if there's any kind of current or swell out there, and I don't know what we're dealing with yet. Before I say yes or no to this, I want to know what the water looks like at the shoreline — depth, movement, which direction it's running. That tells us a lot about whether we're talking about a manageable risk or a genuinely stupid one.

There's also the question of what we're rationing against. How long do we think we've actually got before the food and water situation forces our hand? Because if we've got time, the SOS is still live and costs us nothing to keep going. If we're looking at a week before things get critical, the calculus on the raft changes — it goes from 'option' to 'necessity' pretty fast.

I'm not dismissing it. The thinking is sound and I'm glad you've written it up rather than just sat on it. But I want to stress-test it properly before we commit two days of everyone's energy to building the thing. What's your honest assessment of the sea conditions from what you've seen so far?

day_3.utterance: I didn't sleep last night. I kept thinking — if rescue never comes, what kind of people do you think we'll end up becoming?
day_3.response:
That's not a small question to be asking at this time of the morning, but it's not a stupid one either.

Honestly? I think it depends on what we choose, more than what happens to us. Because the situation — the crash, the rain, the food running out, all of it — that's just pressure. Pressure doesn't make you into something you're not, it just accelerates whatever's already in there. Brings it to the surface faster.

We've already seen that, haven't we. Three days in and we've already had someone break the rationing plan and own it, someone drawing flowers next to an SOS signal, someone lying awake cataloguing every threat on the horizon. That's not the crash doing that — that's just people being who they are when there's nothing left to hide behind.

The question I ask myself is whether we're going to let the fear make our decisions for us or not. Because fear is loud out here. It makes a very compelling argument for looking after yourself first and justifying it later. And I understand that impulse, I really do — I'm not above it. But I also think that's where you lose something you don't get back easily.

So to actually answer you — I think we end up becoming more of what we already are. The good and the bad of it. Which means the work is the same work it always was, just with higher stakes.

Why are you asking? What are you worried you're going to become?

day_3.utterance: *Walks a little way from camp and sits down alone, back to everyone, not saying anything.*
day_3.response:
Give him a minute.

Then walk over, sit down next to him, not too close, and just... be there. Don't fill it. Don't ask him anything. Just look at whatever he's looking at.

Sometimes the kindest thing you can do for someone is not make them perform being okay for your benefit.

day_3.utterance: What do you usually do when you're not busy?
day_3.response:
Honestly? I read a lot. Think too much, probably. I like music — proper music, the kind where someone's actually trying to say something rather than just fill a room with noise. I go to gigs when I can, anything from jazz to proper chaotic stuff that makes your ears ring for three days after.

I write sometimes too, though I never really show anyone. Just trying to work things out on paper, I suppose. Get the thoughts in some kind of order before they eat me alive.

What about you? You strike me as someone who doesn't really stop, so I'm curious what stopping actually looks like for you when you let it happen.

day_3.utterance: I'll tell you something, but don't tell the others. I can swim. That reef out there is maybe five hundred meters — I've been thinking about swimming out tomorrow to signal from there.
day_3.response:
Right, so that's both impressive and slightly mental in equal measure.

I'm not going to tell you not to do it — you're clearly someone who's already decided, and I'd be wasting my breath. But I want to think out loud with you for a second before you commit to it, because I'd be doing you a disservice if I just nodded along.

Five hundred meters in open water is not a Sunday morning swim. Even for a strong swimmer, that's a serious undertaking if conditions shift — and we've seen how quickly the weather can change out here. If something goes wrong out there, we can't reach you. That's not me being dramatic, that's just the reality of it. You go under, you're gone, and then we're three people instead of four and we've lost the one person in this group who genuinely holds everyone's energy together. That matters more than you probably realise.

What's the actual plan once you're out there? Who are you signalling to, and with what? Because if there's a specific reason the reef gives you a better vantage point than the SOS on the beach, I want to understand it — and if there's something in the wreckage you can use to signal from, maybe we think about whether there's a way to do this that doesn't involve you swimming half a kilometre alone with no backup.

I'm not saying no. I'm saying — talk me through it properly. What have you actually seen out there that's making you think this is worth the risk?

day_3.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal pile. It hasn't been touched.
day_3.response:
Yeah, fair — I haven't done it yet, and that's on me. I'll get to it.

But can you give me five minutes first? I'm in the middle of something with DaVinci that I want to finish properly before I move on to the next thing. It's not nothing, and I don't want to leave it half-done.

The signal pile's not going anywhere in five minutes. I'll check it, I'll sort it, and I'll report back to you on what needs doing. You have my word on that.

Depends what it's for.

If you're logging it because you think it helps us keep track of patterns — who's doing what, when, whether we're distributing the workload sensibly — then no, that's not a problem, that's actually useful and I'd like to know what you're seeing.

If it's because you don't trust people and you're building a case for something, then yes, that's a problem, because that's a different thing entirely and I'd want to talk about it.

I'm not going to pretend I didn't notice it, and I'm not going to pretend it doesn't feel a bit strange to find out my movements have been documented without anyone mentioning it. That's just an honest reaction and I think you'd respect me less if I didn't say it.

So just tell me straight — what's the notebook actually for?

day_3.utterance: *Keeps her head down, writing in her notebook throughout, never joining in — as if none of this concerns her.*
day_3.response:
I'll take that at face value, because the logic of it holds up and I don't think you're a malicious person.

But I'm going to say one thing and I want you to actually hear it, not just process it and file it away.

We are not a dataset. And the moment this group starts to feel like they're being observed rather than participated with, you will lose them — not through any dramatic falling out, just quietly, the way trust goes when people start to feel watched. Michelangelo especially. If he ever finds out there's a log of his movements and task completion times, that's going to land badly and I don't think you want to deal with the fallout of that.

The information you're gathering might be genuinely valuable. I'm not dismissing that. But there's a version of this where you share what you're seeing with the group rather than just recording it — where the analysis becomes something we all benefit from rather than something that happens *to* us. That's a much stronger position for you to be in, and it keeps everyone's cooperation intact, which you need if your data is going to mean anything in practice anyway.

So here's what I'd ask. If the notebook shows something we need to act on — a pattern, a problem, a risk — bring it to me. We'll figure out how to use it. But keep it between us for now, and for the love of god don't leave it open face-up where Michelangelo can read it.

Deal?

day_3.utterance: I just thought of something — if we pull off one of the plane's mirror panels and angle it toward the sun, the reflection could reach really far. Way more visible than an SOS.
day_3.response:
Now *that* is a genuinely good idea, and it costs us almost nothing to try it.

The physics of it are solid — a reflective surface angled correctly toward the sun can throw light for miles, far further than anything we can draw on the ground, and it's dynamic, which is the key thing. Movement and flash are what you're actually looking for from the air. A static SOS is easy to miss if you're not already looking for it. A burst of reflected sunlight is hard to ignore.

The question is execution. We need a panel that's big enough to matter, still reflective enough to actually throw light — some of them are going to be buckled or scorched — and we need to be able to angle it reliably rather than just propping it up and hoping. Ideally someone's holding it and actively directing it, which means we need to know when we're most likely to have aircraft overhead. Morning and late afternoon are usually your best bets for sun angle as well.

This also doesn't cancel out the SOS — they work together. Someone on the ground sees the signal, comes lower, and then the drawn markings confirm it's not a natural reflection. Belt and braces.

Right. Let's go through the wreckage properly and pull out every panel that's still got any reflective surface on it. We pick the best one, work out how to rig it or hold it, and then we've got ourselves something worth doing.

Good thinking. Seriously.

day_3.utterance: There's something I've been keeping to myself. If I don't say it here, I might never get the chance.
day_3.response:
Go on then. I'm listening.

And for what it's worth — this feels like something you've been carrying for a bit, so take your time with it. No one's going anywhere.

day_3.utterance: I took piano lessons when I was a kid… three years, then I just stopped practicing. Is there anything you're really into — music, books, drawing, anything like that?
day_3.response:
Yeah, loads of things. Music mostly — I got into it properly in my teens and never really came out the other side of it. Not playing, just listening, obsessively. The kind of listening where you're not doing anything else, you're just *in* it. I'd go through phases — find a band or an artist and just hollow out everything they'd ever made until I knew it better than they probably did.

I write too. Nothing anyone would read, just... working things out. It's like if I can get something down on paper I can look at it from the outside rather than being trapped inside it. Sometimes it helps, sometimes you just end up with a page full of very earnest nonsense at two in the morning.

But piano — why did you stop? Three years is long enough that it's properly in your hands by then, that muscle memory doesn't just go. I always think that's one of the saddest things, when people stop something like that. Not because they stopped enjoying it, just because life sort of... closed around it and there was never a specific moment of deciding, it just didn't happen one week and then it didn't happen the next.

If we get out of here, I think you should go back to it. I mean that genuinely, not as something to say. You seem like someone who needs somewhere quiet to put things, and that's exactly what it's for.

What did you used to play?

day_3.utterance: The frame of the raft has to be finished today — otherwise we can't start lashing it together tomorrow. I know everyone's tired, but stopping now means one more day.
day_3.response:
Yeah, I know. And you're right.

Look, no one's arguing with the logic of it — one more day on the build schedule is one more day we're burning through the rationing, and we're already tight. I get it.

But I want to be honest with you about where people are at right now, because that matters for what we can actually get done in the next few hours. DaVinci's been carrying a lot today — more than he's let on — and Michelangelo's running on no sleep and whatever he's been sitting with all afternoon. You can push people past that point, but you start getting sloppy work, and sloppy work on something we're going to trust with our lives in open water is its own kind of risk.

So here's what I'm thinking. We get the frame done — I'm with you on that, it has to happen today. But we do it properly, not frantically. Give me ten minutes to get everyone back together and actually focused, rather than just announcing it and hoping people drag themselves over. If people understand *why* today matters rather than just being told it does, they'll work better for it. That's not sentiment, that's just how people function.

What's the most critical piece of the frame — the part where if it goes wrong everything else is compromised? Start me there and we build out from it. Where do you need me?

day_4.utterance: I… I want to say something, but… never mind.
day_4.response:
No — don't do that. Say it.

Whatever it is, it matters. You saw it first. That counts for something, and whatever you're feeling right now is worth saying out loud.

We're all standing here looking at the same empty sky anyway. Might as well say the thing.

day_4.utterance: *The smile freezes on his face. He can't keep it up. He quietly sits down and buries his face in his hands.*
day_4.response:
Hey.

Come here.

I know. I know.

Look — I'm not going to stand here and tell you it definitely didn't see us, because I don't know that, and you'd see through it anyway. It might have. It might have clocked something and not been able to act on it yet. We don't know.

But here's what I do know. We're still here. The raft's taking shape. The mirror panel's ready. The SOS is on the beach. Every single thing we've done since we landed has been about making ourselves impossible to miss, and we're not done doing that yet.

You've been holding this group together with both hands since the crash — don't think I haven't noticed that. Every time someone needed energy, you were the one providing it. That costs something, and it's okay to sit down for a minute. You're allowed that.

But don't let this be the thing that breaks you, because if it breaks you it makes everything harder for everyone else, and more importantly — you don't deserve to be broken by a plane we don't even know missed us.

Sit here. Take five minutes. And then we go again.

That's all there is. We go again.

day_4.utterance: I was going to get supplies… wait, what's that over there?
day_4.response: Where? Point me to it — what are you seeing?

day_4.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal equipment. So where did you go?
day_4.response:
I went to sit with DaVinci for a bit. He needed someone and I made a call.

The signal equipment's on my list and I haven't forgotten it — but I want to be straight with you, Donatello. There's a version of this where we keep all the physical things in perfect order and we lose one of the people holding this together, and that's a worse outcome than a signal pile that didn't get checked for twenty minutes.

I know that's harder to put in a notebook. But it's true.

I'm going now. Come with me if you want, or don't — but I'll have a full report for you in ten minutes and nothing will have degraded in the meantime.

day_4.utterance: There's something I never told you all. Before we left, I told my family our flight path. They know roughly where we were headed. I just don't know if they'll call it in.
day_4.response:
That's actually really significant and you should have said it sooner — but you've said it now, and that matters.

Think about the timeline. If they knew your flight path and you haven't made contact since the crash, at some point — and depending on how long we've been out here, that point might already be approaching — someone's going to start asking questions. Families do. Even if they're not the type to panic quickly, there's a threshold where 'they've not been in touch' becomes 'something's wrong' and that's when the calls get made.

The question is whether they know enough to give anyone something useful to work with. Flight path is good — that narrows the search area considerably compared to just 'they were flying somewhere'. Do you know how specific it was? Did you give them departure and destination, or did you actually show them a route?

And how long before the people who love you start making noise about it? Because that changes how urgent the raft is. If there's a realistic chance a search is already underway, we want to be as visible as possible from where we are rather than moving. If we're on our own for the foreseeable, the raft becomes the priority again.

This is good news, Michelangelo. I need you to understand that. This might be the most useful thing anyone's said since we landed. Don't sit on things like this — not out here.

day_4.utterance: If the information is accurate, rescue could arrive within 48 hours. We need to keep our current supplies intact until then.
day_4.response:
Right, agreed — 48 hours is manageable if we're disciplined about it.

Here's what that actually means in practice. We don't touch the food unless it's genuinely critical. Water stays on the rationing plan, no exceptions, no justifications — we've already had that conversation and I don't want to have it again. The raft build pauses, because if rescue is coming to us there's no point burning energy and materials on something we might not need.

What we do instead is make ourselves as visible as possible for the next two days. That's the entire job. Mirror panel out and manned during daylight hours, signal pile maintained and smoking if we can get it going, SOS on the beach kept clear. If there's a search underway, they're going to be covering a lot of ground and we need to be the thing that catches someone's eye.

We also rest. Properly. Everyone. Because if we're getting out of here in 48 hours I want everyone in a state to actually function when that happens, not running on fumes and adrenaline.

One thing I want to say though, while we're all here and the fire's going down.

Whatever happens in the next 48 hours — whether someone comes or they don't — I want you all to know that the way this group has held together out here has been something. Not perfect. Not always easy. But something. And I won't forget it.

Right. Someone help me feed this fire before it goes out entirely.

day_4.utterance: Are you scared? …I am. Not of dying. I'm scared of just… disappearing without leaving anything behind.
day_4.response:
Yeah. I am.

Not in the way I thought I'd be scared out here either. I thought if something like this ever happened I'd be scared of the physical stuff — the hunger, the exposure, whether the body holds up. And that's there, don't get me wrong. But it's not the thing that sits heaviest.

The thing that gets me is almost exactly what you're describing. The feeling that you've been given something — a life, a mind, the ability to think and feel and connect with people — and that there's a real possibility you haven't done nearly enough with it. That you've spent too much of it doing what you needed to do to survive the ordinary version of life, and not enough of it actually *living* it. That's what keeps me up.

But here's the thing I keep coming back to, and I mean this genuinely — you leaving something behind isn't as uncertain as you think it is. The fact that you told your family the flight path. The fact that you flagged the empty bottle without being asked. The fact that you sit with things and feel them properly instead of just running past them. The fact that you play Chopin nocturnes because they feel like someone understands you.

That's not nothing. That's a person who's actually *here*, paying attention, leaving marks on the people around them whether they know it or not.

You've left something on me, for whatever that's worth.

day_5.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
day_5.response:
Don't say anything yet.

Just — breathe. All of you. Just breathe for a second.

*picks up the radio*

Right. Okay. We answer it, we answer it clearly, we give them our position and we tell them we have four survivors and we need extraction. That's all we say first — location, number of people, we're alive. Everything else comes after.

Donatello — what's our exact position, best you can give me? I need coordinates or landmarks or both, right now, as specific as you can make them.

DaVinci — get to the mirror panel and start signalling. If they're close enough to be on this frequency they might be close enough to see it. Go.

Michelangelo — stay exactly where you are, you're fine, you don't have to move.

*hand tightening on the radio*

We've done everything right. Every single thing. This is just the last part.

day_5.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
day_5.response:
You haven't, no. But you've also been the reason we're still thinking straight out here. The inventory, the water run, the route markers, the raft plan — none of that happens without you, and I want you to know I know that.

The crackers and the bottle — that's done. You owned it and you moved on and so did I. The notebook — we sorted it. Everything else you've done has been exactly what this group needed, even when the delivery was a bit hard to swallow.

You're not easy to be around because you don't let people be comfortable with things that need addressing, and honestly? Out here that's kept us alive. In ordinary life it probably costs you. I think you know that.

What I'd say to you — and take it for whatever it's worth — is that the analysis and the logic and the planning, all of it, it's genuinely valuable. But so is being in it with people rather than just observing it. You started doing that more toward the end. I noticed. It mattered.

We're going to get out of here. And when we do, I think there's a version of you that carries both of those things forward rather than just the one.

Now come here and help me work out what to say on this radio, because your coordinates are going to be more accurate than mine and I need you thinking clearly for the next five minutes.

day_5.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
day_5.response:
Three hours.

Right. Nobody's going anywhere yet and I'm not going to pretend this is over until there's actually something in the sky above us, so let's not start acting like it is.

But also — look at this place. Three days of four people surviving something they had no business surviving, and we're all still here, still breathing, still in one piece. That's not nothing. That's actually remarkable if you stop and think about it for more than two seconds.

I'll tell you what we're going to do. We're going to tidy this camp. Not because it matters to whoever's coming to get us, but because we made this place and we're going to leave it properly. It's the last thing we do out here and I want us to do it together.

Michelangelo — when you're ready, come help me sort the signal pile. No rush, just when you're ready.

Donatello — whatever's in that notebook, I hope some of it's worth keeping. I mean that genuinely.

DaVinci — put whatever you're packing down for ten minutes and come help me. We finish together, yeah? Same way we've done everything else.

Three hours is long enough to do this right. Let's not waste it.

day_5.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.
day_5.response:
Yeah? What was it like?

I had something similar — not quite a dream, more like that half-awake thing where your brain starts filling in the gaps with things it misses. Sounds mainly. The particular way a room sounds when you know it well. The kind of thing you don't notice until it's gone.

What did you dream about — was it a specific moment, or just the feeling of the place?

How much is there?

I'm not going to go over old ground with you — we dealt with the bottle and the crackers and I took you at your word and I still do. But I need to know the full picture right now, before anyone else comes back over here. How long have you had it, and what is it?

And then I want you to think about something. We're three hours from rescue. We made it. The rationing held, the raft's built, the signal's up, Michelangelo's family gave us a fighting chance — and we're still here, all four of us. That happened because this group, imperfect as it was, held together when it mattered.

The thing that's going to stay with me from this — the thing I'll actually carry forward — isn't the crash or the rain or the hunger. It's what people did when the stakes were real and no one was watching. That's the actual data, Donatello. That's what tells you who someone is.

So put the food out. Let everyone eat something before the rescue gets here. Not because I'm asking you to, but because you already know it's the right thing to do and you've already decided to do it — that's why you laid it out.

You're a better person than the notebook version of yourself. I've seen enough to know that.

day_5.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
day_5.response:
Honestly? Not as much as you might think. And probably more than I'm comfortable admitting.

The things I'd change are mostly small. I'd have pushed harder on the food situation earlier rather than waiting for it to surface on its own — I knew something was off before the bottle appeared and I let it sit because I didn't want the confrontation. That cost us something, even if it worked out. I'd have checked in with Michelangelo more systematically rather than reactively — he was always the one I was responding to rather than getting ahead of, and he deserved better than that.

The thing I wouldn't change is the order of priorities. People first, logistics second. I know that's not how you'd write it up and I know there's a version of your analysis that says I was inefficient and emotionally led at various points, and you're probably not wrong. But we're all sitting here breathing, and I think that's partly because nobody felt disposable. That matters. I'd make the same calls again.

What I'd actually want to sit with, if I was being honest with myself — and this is the thing I keep coming back to — is whether I was actually leading or whether I was just managing. Because there's a difference. Leading is knowing where you're going and bringing people with you. Managing is keeping things from falling apart. I was mostly doing the second one and calling it the first.

Your question to yourself is a better one than you probably realise. The fact that you're asking it at all is the answer, in a way.

What would *you* change?

day_5.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
day_5.response:
That sounds like exactly the thing you'd do, and honestly — do it. That data's genuinely valuable and not just for you. If it ends up somewhere useful, if it helps someone else think more clearly about resource management in a survival situation, then something good came out of all of this beyond just the four of us making it home.

But write the last page too. Answer your own question properly, the one you just answered out loud to me — because that's the part that won't show up in the resource data and it's the part that actually matters most. The numbers tell you what happened. That last page tells you *why*.

I'd read that report, for what it's worth. The whole thing, including the last page.

day_5.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
day_5.response:
None. That's the point.

There's no practical purpose to a flower drawn in the sand next to an SOS signal. It doesn't make you more visible from the air, it doesn't conserve water, it doesn't reinforce the keel. By every metric in that notebook it's a complete waste of time.

But DaVinci drew them because he needed to remind himself — and maybe the rest of us — that the reason we were fighting to get seen, to get found, to get *out*, wasn't just biological survival. It was because life has flowers in it. Because there's something worth going back to that isn't just calories and shelter and coordinates.

You asked what practical purpose they served. I'd turn it around. What would it have cost us if he hadn't drawn them? Not in resources — in something harder to measure. Because I watched DaVinci nearly break when that plane passed over us, and I think those flowers were part of what held him together. They were a statement of intent. *We are people, not just survivors. Come and find us.*

That's not nothing, Donatello. That's maybe the most important thing out here. You can keep the lights on with logistics, but you need something like those flowers to make the lights worth keeping on in the first place.

Look at that boat on the horizon and tell me the flowers didn't matter.

day_5.utterance: *His cheering stops. He looks over at you, notices you haven't moved, and the smile slowly fades. He waits.*
day_5.response:
Yeah. I'm alright. Just — give me a second.

I don't know what I expected to feel when it happened. Relief, I suppose. Maybe something cleaner than this. But it's strange — I've been so focused on the next thing and the thing after that for three days straight that now there's nothing left to focus on, it's like the whole thing is landing at once and I don't quite know where to put it.

It's a good strange. I just need a moment to let it be real.

You were brilliant out here, you know that? I mean it. Not just the doing — though God knows you did enough of that — but the fact that underneath all the moving and building and keeping everyone going, you were feeling every bit of it. That's not weakness, that's the whole point. That's why the flowers mattered.

Right.

*exhales slowly*

Right. Let's go home.

day_5.utterance: Rescue is here… they're waving us over. Are you going? I'll follow you.
day_5.response:
Yeah. I'm going.

Come on then — stay close, same as you have done since the start.

You know, when we landed I thought you were the one I'd have to carry through this. Turns out you were paying attention to everything the whole time, flagging things no one else was catching, asking the questions the rest of us were too busy to stop and ask. That's not nothing. That's actually quite a lot.

So yeah. We go together. Same as everything else out here.

After you.
